title: Scenes from American History
description: Ten calm, factual scenes from the history of the United States, from the maps of Lewis and Clark to the first steps on the Moon.

lessons.title: The Maps of Lewis and Clark
lessons.summary: Lewis and Clark cross the West in 1804-1806, and Clark turns their daily notes into a new map of the continent.
lessons.text:
In 1803, the United States bought the huge territory of Louisiana from France for about 15 million dollars. Historians often call the purchase a diplomatic coup: with a single agreement, President Thomas Jefferson roughly doubled the size of the country without a war. Yet the purchase raised a practical problem: almost no one in the East had seen the new land, and no reliable map of it existed.

Jefferson had long been eager to learn what lay to the west, so he decided to send an expedition. He chose his secretary, Meriwether Lewis, to lead it, and Lewis asked his friend William Clark to share the command. Jefferson himself oversaw the preparations. He sent Lewis to Philadelphia to study medicine, plants and the stars with the best experts of the day.

Good maps depend on navigation, the science of finding your position and direction. Sailors had practiced navigation for centuries by measuring the height of the sun and stars, and Lewis carried the same instruments, along with a compass and an accurate clock. Clark, whose training in drawing maps was modest, became the main map maker. His daily method was modest too, but it worked. At each bend of the river, he noted the direction with his compass and estimated the distance the boats had traveled.

The trek began near St. Louis in May 1804. Once the boats left, Jefferson could no longer oversee anything. The men spent more than a year traveling up the Missouri River by boat. During the first winter, a young Shoshone woman named Sacagawea joined them, and her knowledge of the land and its languages proved valuable.

In August 1805, the men crossed the Continental Divide, the line of high ground that separates rivers flowing east from rivers flowing toward the Pacific. Jefferson had hoped for an easy route by water. Instead, beyond the Continental Divide lay range after range of mountains, and this part of the trek was the hardest of the journey.

In November 1805, the party reached the Pacific coast and built a small fort among dense forests. The isolation was deep: their homes in the East were thousands of miles away. Clark used this isolation well. Under the dense gray clouds of a wet winter, he turned his notes into careful maps.

The men returned to St. Louis in September 1806, and people in the East were eager to hear what they had found. Their journals chronicle the whole journey, from the weather and rivers to the plants, animals and peoples they met. Clark's great map, published in 1814, was itself a chronicle of the journey. Earlier maps had shown a single, narrow chain of mountains in the West. Clark's map showed a wide and complicated land, much larger than anyone had imagined.

Questions:
Why do historians call the Louisiana Purchase a diplomatic coup?
With a single agreement, Jefferson roughly doubled the size of the country without a war.
How did Jefferson oversee the preparations?
He sent Lewis to Philadelphia to study with the best experts of the day.
What is the Continental Divide?
It is the line of high ground that separates rivers flowing east from rivers flowing toward the Pacific.
How did Clark use the isolation of the winter on the coast?
He turned his notes into careful maps.
How was Clark's map different from earlier maps?
Earlier maps showed a single chain of mountains, but Clark's map showed a wide and complicated land.

lessons.title: Clinton's Ditch
lessons.summary: New York builds the Erie Canal between 1817 and 1825, and the project that critics laughed at becomes a great success.
lessons.text:
In the early 19th century, moving goods across New York State was slow and expensive. A farmer near Lake Erie had to send his grain to New York City over hundreds of miles of rough roads, and the transport often cost more than the grain itself.

DeWitt Clinton, who became governor of New York in 1817, believed the answer was a canal about 363 miles long, from Albany on the Hudson River to Buffalo on Lake Erie. Many people were quick to dismiss the idea, and it is easy to see why. No canal of that length had ever been built in North America, the country had very few trained engineers, and Lake Erie lies more than 500 feet higher than the Hudson at Albany. Critics called the project "Clinton's Ditch."

Work began on July 4, 1817. The workers, many of them local farmers and Irish immigrants, dug mostly by hand. Because they had little machinery, they built their own, including a machine with two huge wheels that pulled the remains of cut trees out of the ground. This simple machinery saved months of labor.

To climb those 500 feet, the builders used locks. A lock is a stone chamber with gates at each end. A boat enters, the gates close, and water is let in or out until the boat reaches the level of the next section. The locks were placed at intervals along the route: at short intervals where the land rose quickly, and at long intervals where it was flat.

The canal opened on October 26, 1825, and its opening was heralded in a remarkable way. Cannons had been placed at intervals all the way to New York City. When Clinton's boat left Buffalo, the first cannon fired; as soon as the next crew heard it, they fired theirs, and the news crossed the state in less than two hours. In New York, Clinton poured a barrel of Lake Erie water into the Atlantic Ocean, and the city celebrated with parades and a great feast.

By almost any metric, the canal was a success. The first metric is price: the cost of shipping a ton of goods from Buffalo to New York City fell from about 100 dollars to about 10. A second metric is money: the canal cost about 7 million dollars, and its tolls paid back the whole sum within about ten years. Few public works of the time were so profitable. A third metric is growth. Towns such as Rochester and Syracuse grew quickly along the canal, and there was much speculation in land, as people bought fields near the route, hoping to sell them later at a higher price. Some of this speculation was profitable; some was not.

Engineers still describe the canal as a great accomplishment. It was an accomplishment not only of its famous governor, however, but of the thousands of workers who dug it by hand.

Questions:
Why did many people dismiss the idea of the canal?
The canal was very long, there were few engineers, and Lake Erie lies more than 500 feet higher than the Hudson.
How was the opening of the canal heralded?
Cannons placed at intervals fired one after another, and the news crossed the state in less than two hours.
How did New York City celebrate?
It celebrated with parades and a great feast.
Why was the canal profitable?
Its tolls paid back the whole cost of about 7 million dollars within about ten years.

lessons.title: A Wire Across the Continent
lessons.summary: In 1861 a telegraph line joins the East and California, and the Pony Express closes two days later.
lessons.text:
In 1860, a letter from New York to California took weeks to arrive. That April, a private company started the Pony Express to make the trip faster. Its riders carried mail between St. Joseph, Missouri, and Sacramento, California, a distance of nearly 2,000 miles. The company advertised that letters would make the journey in about ten days.

The secret was the relay. Along the route, the company built stations roughly 10 to 15 miles apart. A rider rode at full speed to the next station, jumped onto a fresh horse and rode on. After a long day, he handed the mail bag to the next rider, who continued the relay. Riders crossed deserts, mountains and rivers swollen by spring rain. The service was expensive: at first, a letter cost 5 dollars for half an ounce, so people wrote on very thin paper.

Meanwhile, in 1860, Congress passed a law to support a telegraph line across the country. The telegraph sent messages as pulses of electric current along a metal wire. An operator pressed a key to open and close the circuit, and at the other end, the short and long pulses were turned back into letters. Today we know that an electric current is a flow of electrons, tiny particles with a negative charge. The builders of 1861 knew nothing of electrons, which were discovered only in 1897.

Over long distances, a current grows weak, so telegraph lines used relays. A relay is a small switch worked by a magnet. A weak signal moves a light metal arm, which closes a second circuit with a fresh, strong current, and thereby sends the message on at full strength. The points where the metal touched were often made of platinum, a valuable metal that does not rust, so the contact stayed clean after thousands of uses.

The line was built by two teams, namely, one working east from Carson City, Nevada, and one working west from Omaha, Nebraska. On the open plains there were few trees, so long lines of wagons carried thousands of wooden poles over hundreds of miles. Other wagons brought wire, tools and food. Each pole was set in the ground and the wire fixed to its top, thereby carrying the line forward mile by mile.

The two lines met in Salt Lake City, and on October 24, 1861, the first message crossed the continent. It was sent by Stephen Field, the chief justice of California, to President Abraham Lincoln, and it stated that California would remain loyal to the Union. A message that had needed ten days now needed minutes.

Two days later, the Pony Express announced that it would close. Its riders still delivered the mail that was pending, namely, the letters already on their way, and by late November the service had ended. Meanwhile, the number of telegraph messages began to swell, and over the following years it continued to swell.

Questions:
What did the Pony Express advertise?
It advertised that letters would cross nearly 2,000 miles in about ten days.
How did the relay of riders work?
A rider changed to a fresh horse at each station and later handed the mail bag to the next rider.
Why were the points of a relay often made of platinum?
Platinum does not rust, so the contact stayed clean after thousands of uses.
What happened to the mail that was pending when the Pony Express closed?
Its riders still delivered the letters that were already on their way.

lessons.title: The First National Park
lessons.summary: Yellowstone becomes the world's first national park in 1872, and its hot springs, its animals and even its tiny living things prove valuable.
lessons.text:
In 1871, a government survey team led by Ferdinand Hayden spent the summer exploring a high, wild region in what is now the northwest corner of Wyoming. Earlier visitors had described boiling springs and columns of hot water shooting into the air, but many people in the East thought these were tall tales. Photographs and paintings made by the team showed Congress that the stories were true. On March 1, 1872, President Ulysses Grant signed a law that made Yellowstone the first national park in the world.

At the time, much of the West was being sold or given away for farms, mines and railroads. Yellowstone was conceived differently: as public land, protected for the people forever. Few people in 1872 could have conceived how popular this idea would become. Today, the United States has more than 60 national parks, and countries around the world have created their own.

Yellowstone sits above one of the largest volcanic systems on Earth. Rain and melted snow sink deep into the ground, are heated by hot rock, and rise again through cracks and vents in the surface. Some vents release steam; others feed pools of bright blue and green water. The park's best-known landmark, Old Faithful, regularly shoots a column of hot water high into the air. Its eruptions can be predicted reasonably well, so visitors can wait for one reasonably sure of a show.

In the north of the park, a different kind of landmark has formed. Hot water carries minerals up from below. When it reaches the air, it cools and leaves a thin layer of white rock behind, and over the years these layers build wide steps called terraces. The terraces change constantly: new ones grow while old ones dry out and turn gray.

Yellowstone's hot water has also proved valuable to science. In 1966, a scientist named Thomas Brock found tiny organisms living in one of the park's hot springs, at temperatures that would kill most life. Researchers later took an enzyme from them. An enzyme is a substance that a living cell uses to speed up a chemical reaction. Most enzymes stop working when they get hot, but this one does not, so it became ideal for a laboratory method that copies genetic material through repeated heating. Today, this enzyme is used in medicine and research around the world.

The park's animals have a history of their own. By 1930, wolves had been removed from the park. In 1995 and 1996, wolves from Canada were brought back. The return of this predator has had many effects. Ravens, for example, often follow wolves and eat what the predator leaves behind. In the wet fields, visitors may also see cranes, tall gray birds. The cranes return each spring to raise their young.

Early visitors threw coins and objects into the hot pools, and there were no rules for the disposal of trash. Today, the careful disposal of food and trash protects both the pools and the animals.

Questions:
Who signed the law that made Yellowstone a national park?
President Ulysses Grant signed it in 1872.
Why is the enzyme from Yellowstone so useful?
It keeps working when it gets hot, so it is ideal for a laboratory method that uses repeated heating.
What do ravens do near wolves?
They often follow wolves and eat what the wolves leave behind.
Why are there rules for the disposal of trash today?
They protect both the pools and the animals.

lessons.title: The Island at the Gate
lessons.summary: Between 1892 and 1954 about 12 million immigrants pass through Ellis Island, which is later restored as a museum.
lessons.text:
From 1892 to 1954, a small island in New York Harbor called Ellis Island was the main entrance for immigrants arriving in the United States. During its sixty-two years of service, about 12 million people passed through it. The magnitude of this movement is hard to imagine. On the busiest day in its history, in April 1907, more than 11,000 people were examined on the island.

For a new arrival, the process followed a fixed order. A small boat carried people from their ship to the island. They climbed a long set of stairs to the great hall. What most of them did not know was that the examination had already begun. Doctors stood at the top of the stairs and watched each person climb, looking for signs of illness or weakness.

These doctors were experienced medical practitioners, and the magnitude of their task forced them to work quickly. A practitioner might see thousands of faces in a single day. If a doctor suspected a problem, he marked a letter in chalk on the person's coat, and that person was sent for a closer examination.

Next came the questions. An inspector asked each person about his or her name, work, money and plans. Because the immigrants spoke dozens of languages, the island employed interpreters, who translated Italian, Polish, Greek, Arabic and many other languages. Arabic was spoken by many families from what are now Syria and Lebanon. The job required not only language skills but also sensitivity, because the new arrivals were tired and often afraid. A question asked without sensitivity could upset a family after weeks of travel. One young interpreter, Fiorello La Guardia, worked there while studying law at night; he later became mayor of New York City.

Most people passed through in a few hours. Some, however, were held in detention, either for medical care in the island's hospital or for a hearing about their case. Detention could last days or even weeks. Yet most of those held were allowed to enter in the end; only about 2 percent of all arrivals were sent back.

For many, the journey was a choice: they came for work, land or family. For others, it was a form of exile. They had left their home countries because of their religion or their political views, and they could not safely return. For them, exile and a new beginning were the same thing.

Ellis Island closed in November 1954, and its buildings slowly fell apart. Between 1984 and 1990, the main building underwent a major renovation. After the renovation, it opened again as a museum of immigration.

Today, many visitors are the grandchildren of people who climbed those stairs. A grandchild can search the old ship records and find the name of a grandmother or grandfather, written down on the day he or she arrived.

Questions:
How long did Ellis Island serve as an entrance to the country?
It served for sixty-two years, from 1892 to 1954.
Why did the medical practitioners watch people climb the stairs?
They were looking for signs of illness or weakness.
Why did the interpreters need sensitivity?
The new arrivals were tired and often afraid.
Why did some immigrants live in exile?
They had left because of their religion or political views and could not safely return.
What can a grandchild do today?
A grandchild can search the old ship records and find the name of a grandmother or grandfather.

lessons.title: Soldiers in the Sierra
lessons.summary: Before the National Park Service existed, Black soldiers protected Yosemite and Sequoia, and Captain Charles Young built a road to the giant trees.
lessons.text:
Today's park rangers wear the familiar flat hat of the National Park Service. That service, however, was created only in 1916. Before then, the first parks in California, Yosemite and Sequoia among them, were protected by the United States Army.

Each summer from 1891 to 1914, soldiers rode from San Francisco to the Sierra Nevada mountains to patrol these parks. In 1899, and again in 1903 and 1904, some of them were Black soldiers from the 24th Infantry and the 9th Cavalry. Soldiers from these two regiments were known as the Buffalo Soldiers. In the parks, their task was to protect forests and mountain fields.

In 1903, a unit of the 9th Cavalry arrived in Sequoia under Captain Charles Young, the third Black graduate of the military academy at West Point. At that time, the officer in command of a park also served as its acting superintendent, so Young became the first Black leader of a national park.

The soldiers' work was varied. They kept large groups of sheep out of the high fields, where the animals ate young plants down to the ground. They stopped hunting, put out small fires, and built trails and roads. Young's men strove above all to finish a road into the Giant Forest, home of some of the largest trees on Earth. Earlier soldiers had built only a few miles of it. Young's men strove hard, and in a single summer they built more road than had been built in the three summers before.

Visitors who walk among these giant trees often say that the forest feels like a cathedral. The great trunks rise like the columns of a church, and the light falls gently from far above, as it does through the high windows of a cathedral.

The Sierra Nevada rises from low, warm hills to peaks higher than 14,000 feet, and as the altitude increases, the forest changes. The giant trees grow at middle altitudes, roughly between 5,000 and 7,000 feet. Higher up, the air is colder and the summer is shorter. Near the upper edge of the forest, pines are stunted by wind and snow, and some that are hundreds of years old are no taller than a man. In a single day's ride, a soldier could see how altitude shapes life: from giant trees to small, stunted ones.

The army's way of running the parks had strengths and weaknesses. The soldiers were well organized and hard working, but they came only for the summer and left each autumn, and orders from distant officers allowed little flexibility. Supporters of the parks argued that they needed a permanent service with the flexibility to protect each park all year round. In 1916, Congress created the National Park Service, and today its rangers tell visitors the story of the Buffalo Soldiers.

Questions:
Which regiments were known as the Buffalo Soldiers?
The 24th Infantry and the 9th Cavalry, which were made up of Black soldiers.
What did Young's men strive to finish?
They strove to finish a road into the Giant Forest.
Why do visitors compare the forest of giant trees to a cathedral?
The trunks rise like columns, and the light falls gently from far above.
Why are the pines near the upper edge of the forest stunted?
They are stunted by wind and snow at high altitude.
Why did supporters of the parks want a new service?
They wanted a permanent service with the flexibility to protect each park all year round.

lessons.title: One Vote in Tennessee
lessons.summary: After 72 years of campaigning, women win the right to vote in 1920, when a young lawmaker in Tennessee follows his mother's advice.
lessons.text:
In July 1848, about 300 people met in the small town of Seneca Falls, New York, to discuss the rights of women. Among their demands was one that many people at the time considered extreme: the right to vote. Winning it took 72 years.

The campaign followed two roads. The first road led through the states, since each state decides many questions about voting. In many states, a change required a referendum, a vote in which the citizens themselves decide whether a proposal becomes law. Since women could not vote, only men decided these referendums, and the results were often disappointing. Wyoming gave women the vote in 1869, while it was still a territory, and several other western states followed. In the East, however, most referendums failed. In New York, a referendum in 1915 lost clearly. It was a disappointing defeat, but supporters worked even harder, and a second referendum, two years later, succeeded.

The second road led to Washington. An amendment to the Constitution would give the vote to women in every state at once. Opponents raised many objections. One objection was that politics would harm family life; another was that voting should remain a matter for each state. To supporters, keeping women from voting was a denial of a basic right, and the denial of a voice to half the population could not be called democracy.

Not all supporters agreed on methods. Some groups preferred patient work: petitions, letters and quiet meetings with members of Congress. Others thought this approach was too passive. In 1917, women from the National Woman's Party, led by Alice Paul, began to stand outside the White House holding signs. They did not shout, but they were far from passive: they stood there day after day, in rain and in snow.

In 1919, Congress finally passed the 19th Amendment. To become part of the Constitution, it had to be approved by 36 of the 48 states. By the summer of 1920, 35 states had approved it, and the decision came down to Tennessee. The mood in Nashville, the state capital, was tense. Supporters of the amendment wore yellow roses; opponents wore red ones. On August 18, the vote in the lower house was so close that every member mattered, and the room was tense.

Harry Burn, at 24 the youngest member, was wearing a red rose. In his pocket, however, he carried a letter in an envelope from his mother, Febb Burn. In the letter, she asked him to vote for the amendment. Burn voted yes, and the amendment passed by a single vote. Later he explained that a son should follow his mother's advice.

Accordingly, on August 26, 1920, the Secretary of State signed the document that made the amendment law. Election officials prepared accordingly, and that November, millions of women across the country voted for president for the first time.

Questions:
Why were the results in the states often disappointing?
Only men could vote, and in the East most referendums failed.
What objections did opponents raise?
They said politics would harm family life and that voting should remain a matter for each state.
Why were the women outside the White House not passive?
They stood there day after day, in rain and in snow.
What was in Harry Burn's envelope?
It held a letter from his mother asking him to vote for the amendment.
What happened accordingly on August 26, 1920?
The Secretary of State signed the document that made the amendment law.

lessons.title: Painting the Walls of a Nation
lessons.summary: During the Great Depression, the WPA's Federal Art Project pays artists to paint murals in schools, hospitals and libraries.
lessons.text:
By 1935, the United States was in the sixth year of the Great Depression. Millions of people were out of work, and artists were among the hardest hit: when families could barely afford food, few could afford paintings. That year, as part of a large program called the Works Progress Administration, or WPA, the government created the Federal Art Project. Its aim was to employ artists, who would be compensated with a regular wage, to create art for public buildings. Most were paid about 24 dollars a week. For a painter without work, such a job felt like winning the lottery. In fact, it was not a lottery at all: artists had to show both that they needed work and that they had the training to do it.

Many of the project's best-known works were murals, large paintings made for walls. They appeared on the premises of schools, hospitals, libraries and other public buildings.

Some painters used an old Italian method. First, a worker spread fresh, wet plaster over only as much of the wall as the painter could finish in one day. The painter then applied colors mixed with water, and as the plaster dried, the colors became part of the wall itself. Because the wall dried within hours, there was no time to stop and think, and a mistake could not simply be painted over: that section had to be removed and done again.

The shape of the room mattered too. A wall is flat, or two-dimensional, but a skilled painter could create a three-dimensional effect, as if the viewer could walk into the scene.

Many painters had been inspired by the great Mexican artist Diego Rivera, who, from 1922 on, had covered public walls in Mexico with scenes of history and work. The result was a fusion of a Mexican tradition with local subjects: farms, factories, rivers, railroads and small towns.

Most of the paintings showed calm scenes of work and local history. A few showed strikers, workers who had stopped work to demand better pay. Some local officials objected, feeling that a picture of strikers did not belong on the premises of a school.

Not everyone shared the enthusiasm of the project's supporters. Some members of Congress argued that the government should not pay artists at all. In many towns, however, the enthusiasm was real. People came to watch the painters at work.

As the economy recovered and the country prepared for war, support for the project diminished, and it ended in 1943. By then it had produced more than 2,500 murals. Since then, some have been painted over, and the colors of others have diminished after years of poor care. Yet many have been carefully restored, and they can still be seen where they were made.

Questions:
How were the artists compensated?
They were paid a regular wage, most of them about 24 dollars a week.
Why was getting a job not really a lottery?
Artists had to show that they needed work and that they had the training to do it.
Why did a painter have to work quickly on wet plaster?
The wall dried within hours, so there was no time to stop and think.
What was the fusion in many of the paintings?
It was a fusion of a Mexican tradition with local subjects.
Why did support for the project grow weaker?
Support diminished because the economy recovered and the country prepared for war.

lessons.title: Number 42
lessons.summary: In 1947 Jackie Robinson becomes the first Black player in the modern major leagues and keeps his promise to answer insults only with his play.
lessons.text:
On April 15, 1947, more than 26,000 people filled Ebbets Field in Brooklyn, New York, for the first game of the Brooklyn Dodgers' season. At first base stood a 28-year-old player named Jackie Robinson. When he walked onto the field that afternoon, he became the first Black player in the modern major leagues. For more than sixty years, Black players had been kept out of the major leagues and had played on separate teams of their own.

The man behind this change was Branch Rickey, the president of the Dodgers. Rickey had deliberately searched for the right player. He wanted someone with great talent, but also someone with unusual strength of character. Robinson had been a college star in four sports and an army officer, and in 1945 he was playing for the Kansas City Monarchs, one of the best Black teams.

When the two men met in 1945, Rickey asked a hard question. He knew that Robinson would face insults from crowds, from opponents and even from some of his own teammates. What he needed, Rickey said, was a player with the courage not to fight back. Robinson was a proud man with a quick temper, and he had always defended himself. Yet he agreed. For his first seasons, he promised to keep his temper, no matter what happened. He kept that promise, and he answered every insult with his play and with quiet dignity. His dignity under pressure won the respect of many people who had doubted him.

A baseball game is divided into nine innings, and in each of the innings both teams take a turn at bat. Robinson made the innings exciting. Once he reached a base, he deliberately took several steps toward the next one, so that the pitcher had to watch him instead of the player at bat.

Robinson did not get a hit in his first game, and some critics expected him to stumble under the pressure. He did not stumble. By the end of the season, he had led the league in stolen bases and been named the first Rookie of the Year.

In July 1947, Larry Doby joined Cleveland's team and became the first Black player in the other major league. Doby was Robinson's counterpart in that league, and he faced many of the same difficulties as his counterpart in Brooklyn.

Robinson soon became one of the most popular players in the country. Children chewed the gum that came with their packs of baseball cards and hoped to find his picture inside.

Robinson entered the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1962. In 1997, his number, 42, was retired by every team in the major leagues. Every year on April 15, all players wear number 42 in his honor.

Questions:
Why did Rickey deliberately search for the right player?
He wanted a player with great talent and unusual strength of character.
What did Robinson promise to do about his temper?
He promised to keep his temper for his first seasons, no matter what happened.
How did Robinson make the innings exciting?
He deliberately took several steps toward the next base, so that the pitcher had to watch him.
Did Robinson stumble under the pressure?
No, he led the league in stolen bases and was named the first Rookie of the Year.
Who was Robinson's counterpart in the other major league?
Larry Doby was his counterpart.
What came with the packs of baseball cards?
A piece of gum came with them.

lessons.title: A Letter About the Moon
lessons.summary: A grandfather writes to his granddaughter about watching the Apollo 11 landing on television in 1969, when he was a camp counselor.
lessons.text:
Dear Lily,

You asked me what I remember about the day people first walked on the Moon. I remember almost everything, so here is the whole story.

In July 1969, I was 19 and working as a counselor at a summer camp in Vermont. I had loved space since I was 11, when Alan Shepard became the first person from our country to fly into space, in a tiny Mercury spacecraft. Project Mercury sent one man at a time into space. Then came Gemini, with two men, and finally Apollo, with three. In December 1968, the crew of Apollo 8 had flown around the Moon and brought back a famous photograph of our planet rising over the Moon's surface: a blue and white sphere floating in black space.

Apollo 11 left Florida on July 16. Four days later, on Sunday, July 20, two of its three crew members, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin, flew their small landing craft, called the Eagle, down to the surface, while Michael Collins stayed in orbit around the Moon.

The camp had one small black and white television. The other counselors and I carried it into the dining hall and laid an old rug from the office on the floor, and sixty children sat on that rug to watch. In the last minutes before the landing, the voices from the Eagle and from Mission Control in Houston became short and serious. Armstrong had to fly past a field of large rocks to find a safe place, and fuel was running low. We all braced ourselves. Then Armstrong reported in a calm voice that the Eagle had landed, and the hall, which had been utterly silent, exploded with noise.

That was in the afternoon. Armstrong did not step outside until almost 11 at night, and we let the children stay up late. First the hatch of the Eagle opened. Armstrong climbed backward through the narrow hatch and slowly down a ladder. The picture was gray and hard to see, but we could see his boot touch the ground. Next to me, a boy of ten said, "Whoa." Then, as if one word were not enough, he said it again, very quietly: "Whoa." Around 600 million people, roughly a sixth of the world, were watching with us.

I have often tried to describe the thrill of that night. Part of the thrill was simply the danger: we braced for problems until the very end. Part of it was the feeling that something utterly new had happened, and that we had seen it together.

The next morning, I noticed a change at camp. Until then, the younger boys had spent their free time playing cowboys. Now nobody wanted to play cowboys anymore. Everyone wanted to fly to the Moon, and they used the old rug as its surface.

Love,
Your grandfather

Questions:
Where was the writer in July 1969?
He was working as a counselor at a summer camp in Vermont.
What was Project Mercury?
It was the first space program of the United States, and it sent one man at a time into space.
What did the Apollo 8 photograph show?
It showed the Earth as a blue and white sphere floating in black space.
What did Armstrong do when the hatch opened?
He climbed backward through the hatch and down a ladder.
What did the boys stop playing after the landing?
They stopped playing cowboys and wanted to fly to the Moon instead.
